touches.text: Scratch bus: a proof needs a bus it controls (a real store, stub devices, nobody live listening), so the cairn device publishes scratch_bus, the way db_domain's client carries scratch(). Akien 2026-11-12, answering Q#86 (8 proof imports of the bus machine in tester, codemother and librarian, measured 2026-11-11): "works for me". 2.3.8Every device has the panes the base shim defines (17.1.3.5.2), drawn by the web server (15):

A ticket's code is a tool or machine; its life is data. All of its state is on disk, so anyone can instantiate it to talk to it, and any dialog is written to the relevant part of the ticket as it happens. To cross a gate the ticket asks that gate to queue it, sending only its fileref: devices/codemother/0/machines/<inspector>/queueme <fileref>. The gate instantiates the ticket from that fileref on its own side. A ticket instance then processes the pass or fail: on a pass it goes on to the next step, alerting the probes watching the gate (3.3.4.2); on a fail it asks design to queue it, the same way. Self-queuing is the abstract ticket's (3.3.2), so every kind inherits it and no caller queues a ticket on its behalf (Akien, same day: "that could be in the class, rather than the instance :) self queuing"). WHY: Akien, 2026-11-10: "now it has to send it's fileref over to the thing that will process it, and a new code instance created over there even tho it's the same thing... because that's good encapsulation. :)"

There is no central supervisor. Each part starts what it needs by trying to use it: sending a message starts the bus if it is down, a message arriving wakes its shim, the shim wakes its device. Many very small supervisors, each one detect-and-start. WHY: a supervisor is one more thing to keep up, and the system must come up from any part that is touched.
The launcher is Python (bin/cairn), run by Cairn's own interpreter, so Windows needs no bash. Typing `cairn` works on either platform.

Every box runs all the foundational things: a bus, a ground loop, the shims. They are the Cairn device's machines, and there is only one Cairn device: a singleton within the swarm, owning them on every box. WHY: Cairn is the system in aggregate, which is not the same thing as the host (6.6); a box is part of the host, and the swarm of boxes is still one Cairn.

A shim waking its device never takes more than 60 s. A sync caller waits at most 60 s for the wake, then gets "not now" back; a wake that misses 60 s is a trouble. 600 s is the limit for an inference call to come back, not for a wake.

Transport: as fast as we can make it, settled by measuring on this box, not by choosing. Inside a Linux box the bus is our own small broker on Unix sockets, routing by name (measured 50 µs a round trip, against 110 for Postgres NOTIFY and 250 for NATS). Between boxes, and on Windows (Python there has no AF_UNIX), it is TCP, speaking TLS with pinned certificate fingerprints checked both ways; cairn install makes each box's certificate. WHY TLS: no tunnel, nothing extra to set up.
